title: How do you create and manage database users in RDS (standard SQL `CREATE USER`/`GRANT` on the engine, vs IAM database authentication for short-lived token-based logins), and why should applications avoid using the master user?
shortTitle: Creating and Managing Database Users in RDS, and Avoiding the Master User
keyPoints: Create least-privilege database users with SQL CREATE USER and GRANT, giving each service only the tables and operations it needs.
IAM database authentication maps a database user to IAM and authenticates with a short-lived token (about 15 minutes) instead of a stored password.
The master user is a highly privileged admin account meant for setup and migrations, never for everyday application queries.
Using the master user for applications violates least privilege, destroys auditability, makes rotation risky, and turns one leak into total compromise.
Create one dedicated database user per service so permissions and audit trails are traceable per service.
Store passwords in Secrets Manager with automatic rotation when not using IAM authentication.
IAM authentication provides centralized access control through IAM policies and a full CloudTrail audit of every connection.

s1_definition.oneliner: Create least-privilege database users with SQL CREATE USER/GRANT or map them to IAM for short-lived token logins, and never let the application use the all-powerful master user.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **SQL User Management** – Standard `CREATE USER`, `ALTER USER`, and `GRANT`/`REVOKE` commands to create least-privilege accounts on the database engine.
- **IAM Database Authentication** – A feature that maps a database user to IAM and authenticates using a short-lived token (about 15 minutes) instead of a stored password.
- **Master User** – The highly privileged administrative account created when an RDS instance is provisioned, meant only for setup and schema migrations.
- **Secrets Manager** – AWS service that stores and automatically rotates database passwords so they never appear in code or config files.
- **Per-Service Users** – The practice of creating one dedicated database user per microservice so permissions and blame are traceable.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the RDS master user as the bank manager's master key that opens every door at National Bank of India – the vault, the HR files, the server room, everything. You do not hand that master key to a teller who only needs to open one counter drawer. Instead you cut specific keys: a teller key that opens just the cash drawer, a read-only auditor key that opens filing cabinets but changes nothing. IAM database authentication is even safer – instead of a permanent key, the teller is handed a temporary paper pass that expires in fifteen minutes.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌─────────── Database User Management ───────────┐
│                                                 │
│  Master User (locked in Secrets Manager)         │
│  ├── Used ONLY for: CREATE USER, migrations      │
│  └── NEVER used by: application code             │
│                                                 │
│  SQL Authentication Path:                        │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌────────┐ │
│  │ App Code  │──→│ Secrets Mgr   │──→│ RDS DB  │ │
│  │           │   │ (auto-rotate) │   │         │ │
│  └──────────┘    └──────────────┘    └────────┘ │
│                                                 │
│  IAM Authentication Path:                        │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌────────┐ │
│  │ App Code  │──→│ IAM (generate │──→│ RDS DB  │ │
│  │ (Role)    │   │ auth token)   │   │ (SSL)   │ │
│  └──────────┘    │ 15-min expiry │   └────────┘ │
│                  └──────────────┘                │
│                                                 │
│  Per-Service Users:                              │
│  transfer_app ──→ SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE         │
│  report_ro    ──→ SELECT only                    │
│  recon_app    ──→ SELECT, INSERT                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
In RDS I manage database users exactly as I would on a self-hosted engine, because RDS runs the real database engine. I connect once as the master to bootstrap, then I use standard SQL – CREATE USER, ALTER USER, and GRANT or REVOKE – to create purpose-specific, least-privilege accounts. For example I give the transfer service a user that can only select, insert, and update its own tables, and I give the reporting service a user that can only select, so reporting can never modify money. Each service gets its own user with the minimum grants it needs.

The modern alternative to stored passwords is IAM database authentication. I create a database user mapped to IAM and grant the application's IAM role the connect permission, and at connection time the application requests a short-lived authentication token, valid about fifteen minutes, and uses it instead of a password. The benefit is that there is no long-lived secret to store or leak, access is centrally governed by IAM, and every connection is auditable through CloudTrail. When I do use passwords, I keep them in Secrets Manager with automatic rotation.

Applications should never use the master user, and I can give four concrete reasons. It violates least privilege, because the application would have far more power than it needs, including the ability to drop tables and databases. It destroys auditability, because every action looks like the same super-user and I cannot tell which service did what. It makes rotation dangerous, because rotating the master can break administration everywhere. And it turns a single leaked credential into a total compromise of the whole database.

At National Bank of India I created a dedicated user per service on the ledger database – a read-write transfer user, a read-only reporting user, and a reconciliation user – each with only the grants it required, and I locked the master away in Secrets Manager so it was used only by a controlled migration pipeline. For the services themselves I moved to IAM database authentication so there were no stored passwords to leak and every login expired within minutes.

Remember one sentence: Create one least-privilege database user per service, lock the master in Secrets Manager, and prefer IAM authentication so there is no password to leak.
